sources.authority: Government of Alberta
sources.title: English language arts and literature
supports: Grades 4–6 apply grammar, spelling, and punctuation in written communication.
The curriculum includes reading, writing, listening, speaking, viewing, and representing.

sources.authority: Alberta Education
sources.title: Alberta K–12 ESL Proficiency Benchmarks: Grades 4–6
supports: Grades 4–6 writing observations include pronouns, verb tense, plurals, word order, and subject–verb agreement.
Scaffolding and explicit instruction may be appropriate for learners developing academic English.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: subject
supports: A complete sentence has a subject and a predicate.
An imperative sentence normally has the understood subject you.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: predicate
supports: A predicate contains the verb and says something about the subject.
A predicate may also contain modifiers and complements.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: Recognizing clauses
supports: A clause contains a subject and a predicate, unlike a phrase.
A direct command may have an understood subject.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: The structure of a sentence
supports: Sentence length does not determine whether a sentence is complete.
A simple sentence contains one independent clause.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: fragment, sentence fragment
supports: A sentence fragment does not express a complete thought.
Fragments may lack a subject or verb or may be dependent clauses or phrases.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: capitalization: general points
supports: Capital letters distinguish proper nouns from common nouns.
Capitalization practice should be consistent with an identified style.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: capitalization: initial words
supports: Capitalize the first word of a sentence or sentence equivalent.
Capitalize the first word of a direct question.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: The purpose of a sentence
supports: Declarative sentences normally end in periods and direct questions in question marks.
Commands may end in a period or exclamation mark depending on force; polite commands with please normally use a period.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: capitalization: personal names
supports: Personal names are capitalized.
Individual capitalization preferences in names should be respected.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: Capitalization: Family relationships
supports: An unmodified family term is capitalized when it forms part of a name.
A family term used by itself as a name is capitalized.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: capitalization: publications and works of art
supports: The first word of an English title is capitalized.
Short prepositions within English titles may remain lowercase.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: Abbreviations: Canadian provinces and territories
supports: Canadian province and territory names use their official capitalized forms.
Nova Scotia and Alberta are official province names.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: personal pronouns
supports: Subject pronouns use forms such as I, we, he, she and they.
Objects of verbs and prepositions use forms such as me, us, him, her and them.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: Pronoun case: Is it ‘they’ or ‘them’?
supports: Subject and object pronouns take different case forms.
Removing the other part of a compound subject or object is a useful case check.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: prepositions
supports: A preposition is followed by an object.
Between you and me uses object-form pronouns after the preposition.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: Gender-inclusive writing: Use the singular ‘they’
supports: Singular they is accepted in formal writing for a person of unknown gender and for people who use that pronoun.
They remains the subject form and takes plural-form verbs even when its meaning is singular.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: Spelling: When to double the final consonant before a suffix
supports: One-syllable roots ending in a single vowel and consonant normally double that consonant before a vowel suffix.
Multisyllable roots normally double the final consonant when the final syllable is stressed, subject to stated exceptions.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: spelling: words ending in a silent ‘e’
supports: A final silent e is usually dropped before a suffix beginning with a vowel.
A final e after c or g is retained before a or o when needed to preserve the soft consonant sound; noticeable is an explicit example.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: spelling: words ending in ‘c’
supports: Words ending in hard c add k before e, i or y.
Picnicking and panicky are explicit examples of the pattern.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: Suffixes after ‘y’: Keep the ‘y’ or switch to ‘i’?
supports: A final y after a consonant generally changes to i before a suffix.
The pattern has exceptions and should not be presented as universal.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: in-, il-, im-, ir-
supports: The prefix in- changes to im- before b, m or p.
Impossible is an explicit example.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: analyze, analyse
supports: Analyze and analyse are both used by Canadian writers.
Canadian usage shows a growing preference for the -yze form.

sources.authority: Government of Canada, Language Portal of Canada
sources.title: Why Canadian spelling is different
supports: Colour is the generally preferred Canadian form.
Canadian spelling combines conventions from multiple varieties and should be checked rather than inferred from one universal rule.

sources.authority: The National Archives (UK)
sources.title: William Caxton
supports: William Caxton is thought to have brought the printing press to England.
The National Archives dates the first item printed in England by Caxton to 1476.

sources.authority: British Library
sources.title: The Printer
supports: Printing technology emerged in China centuries before it appeared in Europe.
Printing spread through workshops in multiple regions rather than beginning in England.

sources.authority: British Library Archives and Manuscripts Catalogue
sources.title: Add MS 5151: Collections for a history of printing in England, Scotland and Ireland
supports: The collection contains papers, letters, memoranda, drafts, amendments, and printer-related records.
The catalogue documents later handwritten correction and copying within collections about printing history.
